decks.title: Government Budget and Deficits — Part 1: The Budget and its Components
goals: Explain the meaning of a government budget and distinguish the Union budget from State budgets
Classify budgets as balanced, surplus or deficit
Classify receipts and expenditure as revenue or capital, using the liability and asset tests

slides.heading: The Budget and its Components
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what a **budget** is, the **Union and State** budgets, and the **four heads** every item falls under.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: meaning of a budget, Union and State budgets, balanced, surplus and deficit budgets, revenue and capital receipts, and revenue and capital expenditure
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every year governments announce what they expect to collect and what they plan to spend. That plan is the budget. In this part we learn what a budget is, how the Union and State budgets differ, and how every rupee coming in and going out is sorted into revenue or capital. These sorting rules are the key to the deficits in Part 2.

slides.heading: What is a government budget?
slides.body_md: A **government budget** is the **annual statement of estimated receipts and expenditure** of a government for the coming **financial year** (1 April to 31 March).

rows: Covers one financial year, 1 April to 31 March
Figures are forecasts made before the year begins
No tax collected or money spent without approval
States how any shortfall will be financed

visual.alt: Table of features of a government budget: it is annual, it shows estimates, it needs the approval of the legislature, and it shows how any gap will be financed

slides.narration: A budget is a forecast, made before the year starts, of how much money the government expects to receive and how it plans to spend it. Because it is prepared in advance, its figures are estimates. It must be approved by the legislature, and it also shows how any shortfall will be met.

slides.heading: Union and State budgets
columns:
**Union budget**

- Prepared by the **Union government**
- Presented in **Parliament**
- Covers defence, railways and other Union subjects

**State budget**

- Prepared by each **State government**
- Presented in the **State legislature**
- Covers police, State roads and other State subjects

rows: Union subjects such as defence and railways
State subjects such as police and State roads

visual.alt: Table comparing the Union budget and a State budget: who prepares it, where it is presented, its constitutional name and the subjects it covers

slides.narration: India has a federal structure, so there is not one budget but many. The Union government presents its budget in Parliament, and each State presents its own in its legislature. The Constitution does not use the word budget at all; it calls each of them the annual financial statement.

slides.heading: Quick check: what the Constitution calls it
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank: the Constitution calls the Union budget the annual ___ statement.
slides.narration: Recall the name the Constitution uses in place of the word budget.

slides.heading: Balanced, surplus and deficit budgets
slides.body_md: Compare **receipts other than borrowing** with **expenditure**.

visual.alt: Table of three imagined budgets: Tungapur 5,200 against 4,900, a surplus budget; Malini 3,600 against 3,600, a balanced budget; Dhaulagiri 2,750 against 3,100, a deficit budget

slides.narration: Budgets are grouped by comparing what the government expects to receive, leaving out borrowing, with what it plans to spend. If the two are equal, the budget is balanced. If receipts are larger, it is a surplus budget. If spending is larger, it is a deficit budget, and the gap has to be borrowed.

slides.heading: Two parts and four heads

visual.alt: Flow of the structure of a budget: the budget splits into a revenue budget, holding revenue receipts and revenue expenditure, and a capital budget, holding capital receipts and capital expenditure
visual.caption: Two parts, four heads

slides.narration: Every budget has two parts. The revenue budget holds revenue receipts and revenue expenditure. The capital budget holds capital receipts and capital expenditure. So every item you meet belongs to one of four heads, and two simple tests decide which.

slides.heading: Revenue receipts
slides.body_md: **Revenue receipts** neither **create a liability** nor **reduce an asset** of the government.

rows: Income tax, corporation tax, GST, customs duty
Fees, fines, interest received, dividends, grants received
No liability created, no asset reduced

visual.alt: Table of revenue receipts: tax revenue such as income tax and customs duty, and non-tax revenue such as fees, fines, interest and dividends, neither of which creates a liability or reduces an asset

slides.narration: Revenue receipts are money the government receives without owing anything back and without giving up anything it owns. They come in two kinds. Tax revenue includes income tax and the goods and services tax. Non-tax revenue includes fees, fines, interest the government receives and dividends from its companies.

slides.heading: Quick check: a non-tax receipt
slides.body_md: Which of the following is a NON-TAX revenue receipt?
slides.narration: Remember that a fee is paid for a particular service, while a tax is not.

slides.heading: Capital receipts
slides.body_md: **Capital receipts** either **create a liability** or **reduce an asset**.

rows: Borrowing from the public, banks or abroad
Disinvestment (sale of shares in public companies)

visual.alt: Table of capital receipts: borrowing creates a liability, while recovery of loans and disinvestment reduce assets

slides.narration: Capital receipts pass at least one of two tests. Borrowing brings in money but creates a liability, because it must be repaid. Recovery of loans and disinvestment bring in money by reducing what the government owns: a claim on a borrower, or shares in a public company.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classifying the receipts of imagined Hemkunt
slides.body_md: Sort six receipts using two questions.
bullets: **Does it create a liability?** If yes, it is a capital receipt.
**Does it reduce an asset?** If yes, it is a capital receipt.
If **neither**, it is a revenue receipt: a tax or a non-tax item.
Always write the **reason** with the head.

rows: Loan repaid by a city council
Dividend from a state dairy company
Sale of shares in a state hotel company

visual.alt: Table classifying six imagined receipts of Hemkunt: stamp duty, fines and a dividend are revenue receipts; bonds sold, a loan repaid by a city council and a share sale are capital receipts, with the reason for each
visual.caption: Ask two questions: does it create a liability? does it reduce an asset?

slides.narration: Let us sort six receipts of an imagined state. Stamp duty is a tax, so it is revenue. Fines and a dividend from its dairy company create no liability and reduce no asset, so they are non-tax revenue. Bonds create a liability, while a loan repaid by a city council and a share sale reduce assets, so those three are capital receipts.

slides.heading: Revenue expenditure
slides.body_md: **Revenue expenditure** neither **creates an asset** nor **reduces a liability**.

rows: No asset created, no liability reduced

visual.alt: Table of revenue expenditure: salaries, pensions, interest, subsidies and grants given, none of which creates an asset or reduces a liability

slides.narration: Revenue expenditure keeps the government running from day to day. Salaries, pensions, interest on its debt and subsidies create nothing the government owns, and they do not reduce what it owes. Grants given to other governments are also revenue expenditure for the giver, because the giver gets no asset in return.

slides.heading: Quick check: a loan comes back
slides.body_md: True or false: when a government recovers a loan, its liabilities increase.
slides.narration: Ask whether a recovered loan changes what the government owes, or what it owns.

slides.heading: Capital expenditure
slides.body_md: **Capital expenditure** either **creates an asset** or **reduces a liability**.

visual.alt: Table of capital expenditure: building roads, dams and hospitals or buying shares and giving loans creates assets, and repaying loans reduces a liability

slides.narration: Capital expenditure builds or buys things that last, like roads, dams and hospitals, or financial assets such as shares and loans given to others. Repaying borrowed money is also capital expenditure, because it reduces what the government owes.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: classifying the spending of imagined Hemavati
slides.body_md: Sort six items of spending.
bullets: **Does it create an asset?** Then capital expenditure.
**Does it reduce a liability?** Then capital expenditure.
If **neither**, it is revenue expenditure.
Interest and repayment differ: interest is **revenue**, repayment is **capital**.

rows: Loan to a farmers' cooperative bank

visual.alt: Table classifying six imagined items of Hemavati spending: wages, a food subsidy and interest are revenue expenditure; a metro line, a loan to a cooperative bank and repaying bonds are capital expenditure, with reasons
visual.caption: Ask: does it create an asset? does it reduce a liability?

slides.narration: Now the spending side. Wages of forest guards, a food subsidy and interest on old bonds create no asset, so they are revenue expenditure. A metro line creates a physical asset, a loan to a cooperative bank creates a financial asset, and repaying old bonds reduces a liability, so those three are capital expenditure. Notice that interest and repayment of the same bonds fall under different heads.

slides.heading: Quick check: interest received
slides.body_md: How should interest received on loans given to provinces be classified?
slides.narration: Interest received is not the loan coming back, so apply the two tests to it.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: A budget is the **annual statement of estimated receipts and expenditure**.
Union budget in **Parliament**; State budgets in **State legislatures**.
Capital receipts **create a liability or reduce an asset**; revenue receipts do neither.
Capital expenditure **creates an asset or reduces a liability**; revenue expenditure does neither.

visual.alt: Summary table of the four budget heads and their tests

slides.narration: Let us sum up. A budget is an annual plan of estimated receipts and spending, approved by the legislature. The Union and each State present their own. Two tests sort every item: a capital receipt creates a liability or reduces an asset, and capital expenditure creates an asset or reduces a liability. Anything that passes neither test is revenue.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: **Interest paid** is revenue expenditure; **repayment** of the loan is capital expenditure.
**Interest received** is a revenue receipt; **recovery** of the loan is a capital receipt.
A **grant given** is revenue expenditure for the giver, even if the receiver builds assets.
Always state the **reason** (the test) with the head: it earns the mark.
slides.narration: Four traps cost marks here. Interest and repayment of the same loan fall under different heads, on both the paying and the receiving side. A grant given is revenue expenditure for the giver. And never write a head without the reason, because the test is what the examiner rewards.

decks.title: Government Budget and Deficits — Part 2: Measures of Deficit
goals: Calculate the revenue, fiscal and primary deficits from budget data
Explain what each deficit shows about a government's borrowing
Evaluate the implications of high deficits for debt, interest and the economy

slides.heading: Measures of Deficit
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **revenue**, **fiscal** and **primary** deficits: how to calculate them and what they tell us.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: revenue deficit, fiscal deficit, primary deficit, their implications, and the quality of borrowing
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: When a government spends more than it receives, the gap can be measured in three ways. Each measure answers a different question about borrowing. In this part we calculate all three, see what each one reveals, and judge when a deficit is a real worry.

slides.heading: Three measures of deficit
slides.body_md: Each deficit compares different parts of the budget.

rows: Total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts)

visual.alt: Table of the three deficits: the revenue deficit is revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts, the fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus revenue and non-debt capital receipts, and the primary deficit is the fiscal deficit minus interest

slides.narration: The revenue deficit looks only at the revenue account. The fiscal deficit looks at the whole budget, leaving out borrowing from the receipts, so it equals what must be borrowed. The primary deficit takes the fiscal deficit and removes interest on past loans.

slides.heading: Revenue deficit
slides.body_md: **Revenue deficit** = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.
bullets: It shows the government spending **more than its current income** on **current needs**.
The gap is met by **borrowing or selling assets**.

nodes.label: Borrow or sell assets for current needs

visual.alt: Flow of what a revenue deficit implies: current spending above current income is met by borrowing or selling assets, debt grows without new assets, interest rises later and the deficit deepens
visual.caption: Revenue deficit

slides.narration: The revenue deficit is the gap between revenue spending and revenue income. When it is positive, the government is paying for salaries, subsidies and interest partly with borrowed money or by selling what it owns. That borrowing builds no new assets.

slides.heading: Quick check: a revenue gap
slides.body_md: Find the revenue deficit of imagined Shailpur.
slides.narration: Subtract revenue receipts from revenue expenditure.

slides.heading: Fiscal deficit
slides.body_md: **Fiscal deficit** = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts).

visual.alt: Flow of the fiscal deficit: from total expenditure take away revenue receipts and non-debt capital receipts; the gap left is the fiscal deficit, which is filled by borrowing
visual.caption: Fiscal deficit = borrowing

slides.narration: The fiscal deficit takes everything the government spends, on both accounts, and subtracts every receipt that does not create debt. Whatever is left must be borrowed. So the fiscal deficit is exactly the government's borrowing requirement for the year.

slides.heading: Primary deficit
slides.body_md: **Primary deficit** = fiscal deficit − interest payments.

visual.alt: Table of primary deficits of three imagined governments in crore rupees: Hemavati 1,400 minus 900 is 500; Kanakdesh 520 minus 520 is zero; Revapur 960 minus 750 is 210
visual.caption: A zero primary deficit means all borrowing pays interest on past debt.

slides.narration: Part of each year's borrowing only pays interest on loans taken in earlier years. Removing that interest leaves the primary deficit, which shows how much is borrowed for present programmes. When it is zero, every rupee borrowed goes to pay interest on old debt.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the three deficits of imagined Hemavati
slides.body_md: Work through the formulas in order.
bullets: Revenue receipts = 3,000; **revenue deficit = 700**.
Total expenditure = 4,800; non-debt receipts = 3,400.
**Fiscal deficit = 1,400**, equal to borrowing.
**Primary deficit = 1,400 − 900 = 500**.

visual.alt: Table of the worked calculation for the imagined Republic of Hemavati: revenue receipts 3,000, revenue deficit 700, total expenditure 4,800, non-debt receipts 3,400, fiscal deficit 1,400 and primary deficit 500 crore rupees

slides.narration: Take the imagined Republic of Hemavati. Revenue receipts are three thousand crore against revenue spending of three thousand seven hundred, a revenue deficit of seven hundred. Total spending is four thousand eight hundred, and receipts that create no debt are three thousand four hundred, so the fiscal deficit is fourteen hundred. Removing nine hundred of interest leaves a primary deficit of five hundred.

slides.body_md: Arrange Hemavati's three deficits from the smallest to the largest.

slides.heading: What a high fiscal deficit implies
slides.body_md: Persistent fiscal deficits **pile up debt**.

nodes.label: Debt trap; risk of inflation if money is printed

visual.alt: Flow of what a persistent fiscal deficit implies: debt piles up, interest takes more revenue, new loans are needed to pay interest, leading to a debt trap and a risk of inflation if money is printed
visual.caption: Fiscal deficit

slides.narration: One year of borrowing adds to the government's debt, and every later year must pay interest on it. If deficits continue, interest takes a growing share of revenue, and new loans may be needed just to pay that interest. That is a debt trap. If the gap is met by borrowing from the central bank, new money can also push prices up.

slides.heading: Quick check: borrowing equals the gap
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank: the fiscal deficit equals the total ___ requirement.
slides.narration: Think about how the gap in the budget is filled.

slides.heading: Is every deficit bad?
columns:
**Worrying when**

- borrowing pays for **salaries and subsidies**
- **interest** takes a growing share of revenue
- the gap is met by **printing money**

**Can be useful when**

- borrowing builds **roads, power and canals**
- the economy is in a **slump** and demand is low
- new assets **raise future income**

slides.narration: A deficit is not good or bad in itself. What matters is what the borrowing pays for. Borrowing for salaries and subsidies leaves debt without assets. Borrowing for canals and roads, especially in a slump, can lift output and future revenue. Compare two imagined states: one borrows only for assets, the other spends half its borrowing on current needs.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a revenue surplus with a fiscal deficit in imagined Neelachal
slides.body_md: Can a state have both? Yes.
bullets: Revenue surplus = 1,850 − 1,700 = **150**.
Primary deficit = 400 − 300 = **100**.
All the borrowing goes into **assets**, so its quality is good.

slides.narration: This imagined state earns more on its revenue account than it spends there, a surplus of one hundred and fifty crore. But it plans capital works of six hundred and fifty crore, more than its surplus and non-debt receipts together. So it still borrows four hundred crore, all of it for canals and a college. That is a deficit worth having.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: **Revenue deficit** = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.
**Fiscal deficit** = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts) = **borrowing**.
**Primary deficit** = fiscal deficit − interest.
Judge a deficit by **what the borrowing pays for**.

slides.narration: Let us sum up. The revenue deficit shows borrowing for current spending, the fiscal deficit shows total borrowing, and the primary deficit shows borrowing for present programmes after interest. High deficits pile up debt and interest. But borrowing that builds assets is far less worrying than borrowing to pay salaries.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Never include **borrowing** among the receipts when calculating the fiscal deficit.
Include **recovery of loans and disinvestment** as non-debt capital receipts.
Primary deficit **subtracts** interest; it is **smaller** than the fiscal deficit.
For implications, link each deficit to **debt, interest and assets**.
slides.narration: Four points save marks. Leave borrowing out of the receipts when you calculate the fiscal deficit. Remember that recovery of loans and disinvestment count as receipts that create no debt. Subtract interest to get the primary deficit. And when asked about implications, connect the deficit to debt, interest and whether assets are created.

sections.heading: 1. The government budget; Union and State budgets
sections.body_md:
- **Meaning**: the annual statement of a government's **estimated receipts and expenditure** for the coming **financial year**, which runs from **1 April to 31 March**. The Constitution calls it the **annual financial statement** (Article 112 for the Union, Article 202 for the States).
- **Features**: prepared **in advance**, so its figures are **estimates**; must be **approved by the legislature**; shows how any **gap** will be financed.
- **Union budget**: presented by the Union government in **Parliament**; Union subjects such as defence and railways.
- **State budget**: presented by a State government in its **legislature**; State subjects such as police and State roads.
- **Types**: compare receipts other than borrowing with expenditure: **balanced** (equal), **surplus** (receipts larger), **deficit** (expenditure larger, gap borrowed).

sections.heading: 2. Revenue receipts
sections.body_md:
- **Test**: a revenue receipt **neither creates a liability nor reduces an asset**.
- **Tax revenue**: income tax, corporation tax, the goods and services tax, customs duties: compulsory and never repaid.
- **Non-tax revenue**: **fees** and fines, **interest received** on loans given, **dividends and profits** of public enterprises, and **grants received** from other governments.
- Note: interest **received** is revenue, but the **recovery of the loan** itself is capital.

sections.heading: 3. Capital receipts
sections.body_md:
- **Test**: a capital receipt **either creates a liability or reduces an asset**.
- **Borrowings** (market loans, loans from banks and abroad): create a liability.
- **Recovery of loans** given earlier: reduces an asset (the claim).
- **Disinvestment**, the sale of shares in public-sector enterprises: reduces an asset.
- Recovery of loans and disinvestment are **non-debt capital receipts**: they bring in money without creating debt, which matters for the fiscal deficit.

sections.heading: 4. Revenue and capital expenditure
sections.body_md:
- **Revenue expenditure** neither **creates an asset** nor **reduces a liability**: salaries, pensions, **interest paid**, subsidies, and **grants given** to other governments (even if the receiver builds assets with them).
- **Capital expenditure** either **creates an asset** or **reduces a liability**: building roads, dams and hospitals; buying shares; **giving loans**; **repaying loans**.
- The same loan can appear four ways: borrowing it (capital receipt), paying interest on it (revenue expenditure), repaying it (capital expenditure), and, for the lender, receiving interest (revenue receipt).

- **Revenue deficit** = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.
- **Fiscal deficit** = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts). It equals the year's **borrowing**.
- **Primary deficit** = fiscal deficit − interest payments.

- Imagined **Neelachal**: a revenue **surplus** of 150 but a fiscal deficit of 400, because capital spending exceeds the surplus and non-debt receipts.
- Imagined **Kanakdesh**: fiscal deficit 520 and interest 520, so the primary deficit is **zero**.

sections.heading: 6. Implications of deficits
sections.body_md:
- **Revenue deficit**: the government **dissaves**, using borrowing or asset sales for current needs; debt grows **without creating assets**, and future interest rises.
- **Fiscal deficit**: shows total borrowing; if persistent, **debt and interest pile up**, leading towards a **debt trap**; if met by borrowing from the central bank, it can cause **inflation**.
- **Primary deficit**: shows borrowing for **present programmes**; a fiscal deficit close to the interest bill means old debt is driving new borrowing.
- **Quality of borrowing**: imagined Saraswatipur uses 50 per cent of its borrowing for the revenue gap; imagined Neelachal uses none. Borrowing that builds assets, or that lifts demand in a slump, is far less harmful.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Counting borrowing as a receipt when calculating the fiscal deficit.
- Leaving recovery of loans or disinvestment out of non-debt capital receipts.
- Calling interest paid capital expenditure, or repayment of a loan revenue expenditure.
- Classifying a grant given by the Union as capital expenditure because the receiver builds assets.
- Adding interest to get the primary deficit: it is subtracted.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a correct option, a classification or a one-step calculation.
- 2 marks: two points, or a head with its reason.
- 3 marks: three points, or three calculations shown step by step.
- 5 marks (and ISC 4- and 8-mark questions): parts answered separately, formulas written out, and a reasoned comment on what the deficits show.

All governments and figures in SOYL practice are imagined; no actual budget figures are used.

questions.stem_md: A student in an imagined Shimla school is asked to define a government budget. The best definition is

options.text_md: a record of the actual income and spending of all households in the country
a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the government for the coming financial year
the list of prices fixed by the government for essential goods
the total amount of money printed by the central bank in a year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the government for the coming financial year. A budget is an annual statement of estimates for the year ahead. It is not a household account, a price list or a record of money printed.

questions.stem_md: For a budget presented by the Union government of India, the financial year to which it applies runs

options.text_md: from 1 January to 31 December
from 1 July to 30 June
from 15 August to 14 August
from 1 April to 31 March

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** from 1 April to 31 March. India's financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March; the calendar year and the other periods are not used for the budget.

questions.stem_md: The imagined state of Hemkunt prepares its own budget for schools, police and state roads. That budget is presented

options.text_md: in the state legislature, by the state government
in Parliament, by the Union Finance Minister
to the central bank, which approves it
to the Comptroller and Auditor General before it is spent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** in the state legislature, by the state government. Each State presents its own budget, its annual financial statement, in its legislature. Parliament considers the Union budget; the central bank and the auditor do not pass State budgets.

questions.stem_md: The finance minister of an imagined island republic, Malini, expects receipts other than borrowing of ₹3,600 crore and plans spending of exactly ₹3,600 crore. Her budget is

options.text_md: a surplus budget
a deficit budget
a balanced budget
a supplementary budget

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a balanced budget. When estimated receipts (other than borrowing) equal estimated expenditure, the budget is balanced. A surplus needs receipts above spending; a deficit needs spending above receipts.

questions.stem_md: Tungapur (imagined) expects receipts other than borrowing of ₹5,200 crore and spending of ₹4,900 crore. Which statement about its budget is correct?

options.text_md: It is a deficit budget, with a deficit of ₹300 crore
It is a balanced budget, because both figures are estimates
It is a surplus budget, with a surplus of ₹300 crore
It cannot be classified until the year is over

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It is a surplus budget, with a surplus of ₹300 crore. Receipts exceed expenditure by 5,200 − 4,900 = 300 crore, so the budget is in surplus. Budgets are classified on the estimates, before the year ends.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The amounts actually collected and spent by the imagined government of Hemkunt can differ from its budget figures.

**Reason (R):** A budget is prepared before the financial year begins, so it shows estimates rather than actual amounts.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: because the budget is a set of advance estimates, actual receipts and spending can turn out higher or lower.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The figures in the budget that an imagined state, Vaigai Pradesh, presents in March are estimates for the year about to begin.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. A budget is an advance statement of estimated receipts and expenditure for the coming financial year.

questions.stem_md: The Constitution of India does not use the word budget; it calls the yearly statement of the Union government's estimated receipts and expenditure the annual ___ statement.
questions.solution_md: It is the annual financial statement (Article 112 for the Union; Article 202 for the States).

questions.stem_md: A newspaper in an imagined town confuses the Union budget with a State budget. Distinguish the two.
questions.solution_md: Which government, which house, which subjects.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Union budget** is the annual financial statement of the **Union government**, presented in **Parliament**; it covers defence, railways and other Union subjects. A **State budget** is prepared by a **State government** and presented in the **State legislature**; it covers State subjects such as police and State roads.

questions.stem_md: Why is a government budget described as a statement of estimates? Answer with reference to the imagined state of Vaigai Pradesh, which presents its budget in March.
questions.solution_md: Prepared in advance; actuals come later.

answer.model_answer_md: Vaigai Pradesh prepares its budget **before** the year from 1 April begins. Tax collections, prices and needs during the year are not yet known, so the figures are **forecasts**. The **actual** amounts are known only after the year ends and may differ.

questions.stem_md: Explain the meaning of a government budget and give two of its features, as a finance officer of the imagined state of Hemkunt would explain them to new recruits.
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus two features.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Meaning**: a government budget is the **annual statement** of the government's **estimated receipts and expenditure** for the coming financial year (1 April to 31 March).
**Features**: (1) it is prepared **in advance**, so its figures are **estimates**; (2) it must be **approved by the legislature** before the government can collect and spend; it also shows **how any gap will be financed**.

questions.stem_md: Classify the budgets of three imagined governments (₹ crore), giving the size of any gap: Tungapur — receipts other than borrowing 5,200, expenditure 4,900; Malini — 3,600 and 3,600; Dhaulagiri — 2,750 and 3,100.
questions.solution_md: Compare the two figures for each government.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Tungapur**: receipts exceed spending by 5,200 − 4,900 = ₹300 crore, a **surplus budget**.
**Malini**: receipts equal spending, a **balanced budget**.
**Dhaulagiri**: spending exceeds receipts by 3,100 − 2,750 = ₹350 crore, a **deficit budget**, which must be met by borrowing.

questions.stem_md: Which of these receipts of the imagined Republic of Hemavati is a revenue receipt?

options.text_md: Dividends received from a government-owned power company
A loan raised from the public by selling bonds
Money received from selling part of its shares in a state-owned airline
Repayment by a province of a loan the Republic had given it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Dividends received from a government-owned power company. Dividends neither create a liability nor reduce an asset, so they are a revenue (non-tax) receipt. Borrowing creates a liability; selling shares and recovering a loan reduce assets, so those three are capital receipts.

questions.stem_md: The imagined government of Revapur sells 20 per cent of its shares in a public-sector steel company to private investors. In its budget, the money received is

options.text_md: a revenue receipt, because no liability is created
a tax receipt, because companies pay it
revenue expenditure, because the company is transferred
a capital receipt, because it reduces the government's assets

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a capital receipt, because it reduces the government's assets. Disinvestment reduces the government's financial assets (its shareholding), so the proceeds are a capital receipt. They are not a tax, and receipts are never classed as expenditure.

questions.stem_md: Why is money that the imagined Union of Kanakdesh borrows from the public treated as a capital receipt?

options.text_md: It reduces the government's assets
It creates a liability: the government must repay it
It is a compulsory payment by citizens
It is earned by selling services

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It creates a liability: the government must repay it. Borrowing creates a liability to repay, which is one of the two tests for a capital receipt. It does not reduce assets, it is voluntary lending rather than a tax, and it is not a sale of services.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Union of Kanakdesh had lent ₹200 crore to one of its provinces. This year the province repays ₹50 crore of it. For Kanakdesh this is

options.text_md: a capital receipt, because its asset (the loan given) falls
a revenue receipt, because the money is not borrowed
capital expenditure, because a loan is involved
a tax receipt from the province

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a capital receipt, because its asset (the loan given) falls. Recovery of a loan reduces the government's asset (its claim on the province), so it is a capital receipt. It is not revenue, not expenditure and not a tax.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Union government of Kanakdesh receives interest from its provinces on loans it gave them earlier. In its budget this interest is

options.text_md: a capital receipt
a non-tax revenue receipt
a tax revenue receipt
capital expenditure

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a non-tax revenue receipt. Interest received neither creates a liability nor reduces an asset, and it is not a tax, so it is a non-tax revenue receipt. Only the repayment of the loan itself would be a capital receipt.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a NON-TAX revenue receipt for the imagined government of Hemkunt?

options.text_md: Income tax paid by salaried workers
Goods and Services Tax collected on purchases
Fees charged for issuing driving licences
Corporation tax paid by companies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Fees charged for issuing driving licences. A fee is paid for a specific service, so it is non-tax revenue. Income tax, GST and corporation tax are taxes.

questions.stem_md: A finance trainee in the imagined state of Vaigai Pradesh must decide whether a receipt is a revenue receipt. Which test should she apply?

options.text_md: It either creates a liability or reduces an asset of the government
It is received only once in the life of the government
It is received from foreign governments
It neither creates a liability nor reduces an asset of the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It neither creates a liability nor reduces an asset of the government. A revenue receipt passes both negative tests: no liability created and no asset reduced. A receipt that creates a liability or reduces an asset is a capital receipt; frequency and source are not the test.

questions.stem_md: Which of these items in the budget of the imagined state of Hemkunt is revenue expenditure?

options.text_md: Construction of a new bridge over a river
A loan given to a state-run bus company
Purchase of land for a new hospital
Salaries of teachers in government schools

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Salaries of teachers in government schools. Salaries neither create an asset nor reduce a liability, so they are revenue expenditure. A bridge and land create assets, and a loan given creates a financial asset, so those are capital expenditure.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Republic of Hemavati repays ₹300 crore of bonds that fall due this year. In its budget the repayment is

options.text_md: revenue expenditure, because no asset is created
a capital receipt, because a loan is involved
capital expenditure, because it reduces a liability
a revenue receipt, because bonds are returned

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** capital expenditure, because it reduces a liability. Repaying a loan reduces the government's liability, so it is capital expenditure. It is spending, not a receipt, and it does reduce a liability, so it is not revenue expenditure.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Union of Kanakdesh gives a grant to a province, which uses it to build schools. In the Union's own budget the grant is

options.text_md: capital expenditure, because schools are built with it
revenue expenditure, because it creates no asset for the Union government
a capital receipt, because the province receives money
a loan, because the province must repay it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** revenue expenditure, because it creates no asset for the Union government. A grant is not repaid and creates no asset for the giver, so the Union records it as revenue expenditure, even if the province builds assets with it. It is not a receipt or a loan for the Union.

questions.stem_md: Which item in the budget of the imagined Republic of Hemavati REDUCES a liability of the government?

options.text_md: Repayment of a loan taken from a foreign bank
Interest paid on government bonds
Old-age pensions paid to citizens
Recovery of a loan given to a province

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Repayment of a loan taken from a foreign bank. Repaying a borrowed sum lowers what the government owes, so it reduces a liability (capital expenditure). Interest and pensions are revenue expenditure; recovering a loan given reduces an asset, not a liability.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Proceeds from disinvestment by the imagined government of Revapur are capital receipts.

**Reason (R):** Disinvestment reduces the government's assets, because it gives up part of its ownership of public-sector companies.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: a receipt that reduces an asset is a capital receipt, and selling shares reduces the government's holding.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Interest paid on public debt by the imagined Republic of Hemavati is capital expenditure.

**Reason (R):** Interest payments create new assets for the government.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are false. Interest paid creates no asset and reduces no liability, so it is revenue expenditure; it creates nothing for the government.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Loans given by the imagined Union of Kanakdesh to its provinces are capital expenditure for the Union.

**Reason (R):** Such loans give the Union a financial asset: a claim that the provinces must repay.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: spending that creates an asset is capital expenditure, and a loan given creates a claim to repayment.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Fees for registering land collected by the imagined state of Hemkunt are a revenue receipt.

**Reason (R):** Fees are compulsory payments that every citizen must make, whether or not he takes the service.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: fees create no liability and reduce no asset. R is false: a fee is paid only by those who take the particular service, which is what separates it from a tax.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When the imagined Union of Kanakdesh recovers a loan from a province, its liabilities increase.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Recovering a loan reduces an asset (the claim on the province); it does not change the government's liabilities. That is why it is a capital receipt.

questions.stem_md: Fines and penalties collected by the courts and police of the imagined state of Hemkunt are classed as ___ revenue receipts.
questions.solution_md: They are non-tax revenue receipts: they are not taxes, and they create no liability and reduce no asset.

questions.stem_md: Match each item in the budget of the imagined Republic of Hemavati with its budget head.

options.text_md: Corporation tax collected from companies
A loan raised from a foreign development bank
Construction of a national highway
Old-age pensions paid to citizens

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). A tax is a revenue receipt; borrowing creates a liability (capital receipt); a highway creates an asset (capital expenditure); pensions create no asset (revenue expenditure).

questions.stem_md: Explain the two kinds of revenue receipts of the imagined state of Hemkunt, with one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Tax and non-tax, each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Tax revenue**: compulsory payments imposed by law, for example **income tax** or the **Goods and Services Tax**.
2. **Non-tax revenue**: other income that creates no liability, for example **fees, fines, interest received and dividends** from public enterprises.

questions.stem_md: State the two tests for a capital receipt, with one example of each from the budget of the imagined Republic of Hemavati.
questions.solution_md: Liability created or asset reduced, each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md: A receipt is capital if it **creates a liability**, for example **borrowing from the public** through bonds, **or** if it **reduces an asset**, for example **recovery of a loan** given to a province or **disinvestment** of shares.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish revenue expenditure from capital expenditure for the finance department of the imagined state of Vaigai Pradesh.
questions.solution_md: The asset and liability test, with examples.

answer.model_answer_md: **Revenue expenditure** neither creates an asset nor reduces a liability, for example **salaries, interest and subsidies**. **Capital expenditure** creates an asset or reduces a liability, for example **building a dam** or **repaying a loan**.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Union of Kanakdesh gives a province a grant to build a medical college. How is the grant shown in the Union's budget? Give a reason.
questions.solution_md: Classify from the giver's point of view.

answer.model_answer_md: For the Union it is **revenue expenditure**: a grant is **not repaid**, so it creates **no asset or claim** for the Union and reduces no liability. The college becomes an asset of the **province**, not of the Union.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: no asset for the Union

questions.stem_md: Classify each item in the budget of the imagined state of Hemkunt as a revenue receipt, capital receipt, revenue expenditure or capital expenditure: (i) market loans raised; (ii) land registration fees; (iii) salaries of police officers; (iv) money spent to build a district hospital; (v) sale of shares in a state transport company; (vi) interest paid on old loans.
questions.solution_md: Apply the liability and asset tests to each item.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Capital receipt**: borrowing creates a liability.
(ii) **Revenue receipt** (non-tax): no liability, no asset reduced.
(iii) **Revenue expenditure**: no asset created.
(iv) **Capital expenditure**: a hospital is an asset.
(v) **Capital receipt**: disinvestment reduces an asset.
(vi) **Revenue expenditure**: interest creates no asset.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Republic of Hemavati collects ₹2,400 crore in taxes and borrows ₹1,400 crore. Explain why the borrowing is a capital receipt but the tax collection is a revenue receipt.
questions.solution_md: Liability test applied to each.

answer.model_answer_md: Taxes are **compulsory payments** that the government never repays, so they **create no liability** and **reduce no asset**: they are revenue receipts. Borrowing must be **repaid with interest**, so it **creates a liability** for the government: it is a capital receipt. The two sums bring in cash alike, but only the borrowing leaves a **future obligation**.

marking_scheme.step: Taxes: no liability, no asset reduced

questions.stem_md: The imagined Union of Kanakdesh gives the province of Neelachal a grant of ₹80 crore, and Neelachal spends it on building a bridge. Explain how the transaction appears in each government's budget.
questions.solution_md: Classify from each government's own point of view.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Union of Kanakdesh**: the grant is **revenue expenditure**, because it is not repaid and creates **no asset** for the Union.
**Neelachal**: the grant received is a **revenue receipt** (grants-in-aid create no liability), and building the bridge is **capital expenditure**, because the bridge is an **asset** of the province. One transfer can therefore be classed differently by the giver and the receiver.

questions.stem_md: For a government such as the imagined state of Shailpur, the revenue deficit is measured as

options.text_md: total expenditure minus total receipts other than borrowing
revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts
fiscal deficit minus interest payments
capital expenditure minus capital receipts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. The revenue deficit compares the revenue account only. Total expenditure less receipts other than borrowing is the fiscal deficit; the fiscal deficit less interest is the primary deficit.

questions.stem_md: Which expression gives the fiscal deficit of the imagined Republic of Hemavati?

options.text_md: Revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts
Total expenditure minus total receipts including borrowing
Capital expenditure minus borrowing
Total expenditure minus (revenue receipts plus non-debt capital receipts)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Total expenditure minus (revenue receipts plus non-debt capital receipts). The fiscal deficit is the gap between total expenditure and all receipts that do not create debt. Including borrowing in the receipts would always give zero, since the budget balances in accounting terms.

questions.stem_md: The primary deficit of the imagined government of Revapur is obtained by

options.text_md: subtracting interest payments from the fiscal deficit
adding interest payments to the revenue deficit
subtracting the revenue deficit from the fiscal deficit
subtracting borrowing from total expenditure

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** subtracting interest payments from the fiscal deficit. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments. The other combinations do not measure borrowing for current needs.

questions.stem_md: A journalist reports that the imagined Republic of Hemavati has a fiscal deficit of ₹1,400 crore. This figure tells us

options.text_md: the amount of tax evaded in the year
the interest the government pays on old loans
the total borrowing the government needs in the year
the value of public assets sold in the year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the total borrowing the government needs in the year. The fiscal deficit is the gap that must be filled by borrowing, so it equals the government's total borrowing requirement for the year.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Union of Kanakdesh has a fiscal deficit of ₹520 crore and pays interest of ₹520 crore. What does this show?

options.text_md: Its primary deficit is twice the fiscal deficit
It has a revenue surplus equal to the interest paid
Its primary deficit is zero: all its borrowing goes to pay interest on past loans
It borrowed nothing during the year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Its primary deficit is zero: all its borrowing goes to pay interest on past loans. Primary deficit = 520 − 520 = 0. The whole of this year's borrowing is needed just to meet interest on earlier debt; none of it finances current programmes.

questions.stem_md: The imagined state of Shailpur has a large revenue deficit year after year. Which is the most serious implication?

options.text_md: It borrows to meet current spending such as salaries and subsidies, so debt grows without creating assets to repay it
It has too much money in its treasury
Its capital expenditure must be larger than its revenue expenditure
It will have no fiscal deficit in future

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It borrows to meet current spending such as salaries and subsidies, so debt grows without creating assets to repay it. A revenue deficit means current (consumption-type) spending exceeds current income, so borrowing or asset sales pay for it. The debt grows while no income-earning assets are built, which burdens future budgets. The other statements do not follow.

questions.solution_md: Revenue deficit = 1,510 − 1,240 = 270 crore.

questions.solution_md: Total expenditure = 3,700 + 1,100 = 4,800; receipts other than borrowing = 2,400 + 600 + 150 + 250 = 3,400; fiscal deficit = 4,800 − 3,400 = 1,400 crore.

questions.solution_md: Interest = fiscal deficit − primary deficit = 960 − 210 = 750 crore.

questions.solution_md: 450 ÷ 900 × 100 = 50 per cent: half of the year's borrowing pays for current spending.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the fiscal deficit of a government, and what does it show about the imagined Republic of Hemavati?
questions.solution_md: Definition and what it measures.

answer.model_answer_md: **Fiscal deficit** is the excess of **total expenditure** over total receipts **other than borrowing** (revenue receipts plus non-debt capital receipts). It shows the **total amount Hemavati must borrow** in the year, so it measures its **borrowing requirement**.

questions.stem_md: Explain the primary deficit and what it reveals about the budget of the imagined government of Revapur.
questions.solution_md: Formula and meaning.

answer.model_answer_md: **Primary deficit** = fiscal deficit **minus interest payments**. It shows how much Revapur borrows for its **present programmes**, after setting aside the borrowing needed to pay **interest on past loans**.

questions.stem_md: Define revenue deficit and state one implication for the imagined state of Shailpur, which has one every year.
questions.solution_md: Definition plus one implication.

answer.model_answer_md: **Revenue deficit** is the excess of **revenue expenditure** over **revenue receipts**. For Shailpur it means **borrowing or selling assets to pay for current spending** such as salaries, so its debt grows without creating assets.

questions.stem_md: From the data of the imagined Republic of Hemavati (₹ crore) — tax revenue 2,400, non-tax revenue 600, recovery of loans 150, disinvestment 250, revenue expenditure 3,700 (including interest 900), capital expenditure 1,100 — calculate the revenue, fiscal and primary deficits.
questions.solution_md: Apply the three formulas in order.

questions.stem_md: The imagined state of Shailpur runs a revenue deficit every year. Explain three implications for its finances.
questions.solution_md: Dissaving, debt without assets, future interest.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Dissaving**: the government spends more than its current income on current needs, so it **eats into the savings** of other sectors.
2. **Rising debt without assets**: it borrows or sells assets to pay salaries and subsidies, so **debt grows** while no income-earning assets are built.
3. **Future burden**: larger debt means larger **interest payments** later, which raise revenue expenditure and **deepen the deficit**.

questions.stem_md: Explain three possible effects of a persistently high fiscal deficit on the imagined Republic of Hemavati, and say which is the most serious.
questions.solution_md: Three effects and a reasoned judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Debt and interest**: borrowing every year raises the debt, so **interest payments** take a growing share of revenue.
2. **Debt trap**: if new loans are needed just to pay interest, the government **borrows to service debt**.
3. **Inflation**: if part of the deficit is met by **borrowing from the central bank**, new money can **push up prices**.
The **debt trap** is the most serious, because it feeds on itself and leaves less for development.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Union of Kanakdesh has a fiscal deficit of ₹520 crore and pays interest of ₹520 crore. Explain what its primary deficit shows about its budget.
questions.solution_md: Compute, interpret, and note the burden of past debt.

answer.model_answer_md: Primary deficit = 520 − 520 = **zero**. So **all** of this year's borrowing is used to pay **interest on past loans**; present programmes are fully covered by current receipts. The budget is not adding fresh borrowing for new spending, but the **old debt** keeps the government borrowing; to cut the fiscal deficit it must reduce the debt itself.

questions.stem_md: The imagined state of Neelachal has (₹ crore) revenue receipts 1,850, revenue expenditure 1,700, non-debt capital receipts 100 and capital expenditure 650. Show that it has a revenue surplus but a fiscal deficit, and explain why this is less worrying than a revenue deficit.
questions.solution_md: Two calculations and the asset argument.

answer.model_answer_md: Revenue surplus = 1,850 − 1,700 = **₹150 crore**. Fiscal deficit = (1,700 + 650) − (1,850 + 100) = **₹400 crore**. Neelachal borrows only to **build assets** such as roads and buildings, not to pay salaries, so the debt is matched by **assets that can raise future income**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about the imagined state of Aranyadesh, whose budget (₹ crore) shows: tax revenue 1,600; non-tax revenue 350; recovery of loans 90; disinvestment 60; revenue expenditure 2,300, of which interest 520; capital expenditure 500. [3 + 2]

(a) Calculate the revenue, fiscal and primary deficits. [3]
(b) What does the gap between the fiscal and primary deficits tell us about Aranyadesh? [2]
questions.solution_md: Three deficits by formula; interpret the interest gap.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Revenue receipts = 1,600 + 350 = 1,950. **Revenue deficit** = 2,300 − 1,950 = **₹350 crore**. Total expenditure = 2,300 + 500 = 2,800; non-debt receipts = 1,950 + 90 + 60 = 2,100. **Fiscal deficit** = 2,800 − 2,100 = **₹700 crore**. **Primary deficit** = 700 − 520 = **₹180 crore**.
(b) The gap of ₹520 crore is the **interest on past borrowing**. Of the ₹700 crore that Aranyadesh borrows this year, ₹520 crore only **services old debt**, and just ₹180 crore finances **present programmes**, so earlier deficits weigh heavily on its budget today.

marking_scheme.step: Gap equals interest on past debt

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about the imagined Republic of Hemavati, whose fiscal deficit has risen for three years. [2 + 3]

(a) Explain why a fiscal deficit equals the government's borrowing requirement. [2]
(b) "A rising fiscal deficit is always harmful." Evaluate this statement. [3]
questions.solution_md: Identity of FD and borrowing; a balanced judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The budget must be financed. Whatever expenditure is **not covered by revenue receipts and non-debt capital receipts** has to be met by **borrowing**, so the fiscal deficit and the year's borrowing are the **same amount**.
(b) The statement is **too strong**. A rising deficit is **harmful** when the borrowing pays for **revenue spending** such as salaries and subsidies, when interest eats up a growing share of revenue, or when the deficit is met by **printing money**, which can cause inflation. But borrowing that finances **capital spending** on roads, power and irrigation in a **slump** can **raise output and future revenue**, and may repay itself. So the effect depends on **what the borrowing finances and when**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about the budget of the imagined state of Hemkunt. [2 + 3]

(a) State the tests that separate a revenue receipt from a capital receipt. [2]
(b) Classify, with reasons: (i) a loan raised from a development bank; (ii) a grant received from the Union government; (iii) money spent on buying new buses for the state transport service. [3]
questions.solution_md: Two tests; classify each item with its reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A **capital receipt** either **creates a liability** (like borrowing) or **reduces an asset** (like recovery of loans or disinvestment). A **revenue receipt** does **neither**: taxes, fees, fines, interest and dividends are examples.
(b) (i) The loan creates a **liability** to repay, so it is a **capital receipt**. (ii) A grant from the Union is not repaid and reduces no asset, so for Hemkunt it is a **revenue receipt**. (iii) Buses are **assets** that will serve for years, so buying them is **capital expenditure**; their fuel and drivers' wages would be revenue expenditure.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 3]

(a) Distinguish the fiscal deficit from the revenue deficit. [2]
(b) The imagined state of Saraswatipur has a revenue deficit of ₹450 crore, a fiscal deficit of ₹900 crore and interest payments of ₹360 crore. Calculate its primary deficit and the share of borrowing used for the revenue gap, and comment on the quality of its borrowing. [3]
questions.solution_md: Distinguish; two calculations; a judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **revenue deficit** compares only the **revenue account**: revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. The **fiscal deficit** covers the **whole budget**: total expenditure minus revenue and non-debt capital receipts, so it equals total borrowing.
(b) **Primary deficit** = 900 − 360 = **₹540 crore**. Share of borrowing for the revenue gap = 450 ÷ 900 × 100 = **50 per cent**. So **half** of what Saraswatipur borrows pays for **current spending** rather than assets. This is **poor-quality borrowing**: it adds to debt and interest without building capacity to repay, so the state should cut the revenue deficit first.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about the budget of the imagined Republic of Hemavati. [2 + 3]

(a) What is a government budget? How do the Union and State budgets differ in India? [2]
(b) Explain the four components of a budget, with an example of each. [3]
questions.solution_md: Meaning, Union and State; four components with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A budget is the **annual statement of estimated receipts and expenditure** of a government for the coming financial year, called the **annual financial statement**. The **Union budget** is presented in **Parliament** for Union subjects; each **State budget** is presented in its **State legislature** for State subjects.
(b) **Revenue receipts** create no liability and reduce no asset (taxes, fees). **Capital receipts** create a liability or reduce an asset (borrowing, disinvestment). **Revenue expenditure** creates no asset and reduces no liability (salaries, interest). **Capital expenditure** creates an asset or reduces a liability (building schools, repaying loans).

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about the imagined Republic of Hemavati. [2 + 3]

(a) This year its fiscal deficit is ₹1,400 crore and its interest bill ₹900 crore. Next year the fiscal deficit is expected to be ₹1,550 crore with interest of ₹1,050 crore. Calculate the primary deficit for both years. [2]
(b) A minister says the budget has not worsened because the primary deficit is unchanged. Evaluate this claim. [3]
questions.solution_md: Two primary deficits; judge the claim using the rising interest.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) This year: 1,400 − 900 = **₹500 crore**. Next year: 1,550 − 1,050 = **₹500 crore**.
(b) The minister is **partly right**: borrowing for **present programmes** is unchanged at ₹500 crore. But the **fiscal deficit** rises by ₹150 crore, entirely because **interest** rises from ₹900 crore to ₹1,050 crore. Past borrowing is growing and is now **forcing extra borrowing just to pay interest**, the early sign of a debt trap. So the overall position **has worsened**, even though current policy is no looser.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both subparts about the imagined Union of Kanakdesh. [2 + 2]

(i) Kanakdesh sells part of its shares in a public-sector oil company and also receives interest on loans it gave its provinces. Classify both receipts with reasons.
(ii) Explain why money borrowed from the public appears on the receipts side of the budget but is not counted when the fiscal deficit is calculated.
questions.solution_md: Classify two receipts; explain why borrowing is excluded.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The share sale is **disinvestment**: it **reduces an asset**, so it is a **capital receipt**. Interest received creates no liability and reduces no asset, so it is a **non-tax revenue receipt**.
(ii) Borrowing is a receipt because it brings in cash, but it **creates a liability**. The fiscal deficit measures **how much must be borrowed**, so it compares expenditure with **non-debt receipts only**; counting borrowing would make every deficit disappear.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Excluded because the deficit measures borrowing

questions.stem_md:
Answer both subparts. [2 + 2]

(i) The imagined state of Shailpur has revenue receipts of ₹1,240 crore and revenue expenditure of ₹1,510 crore. Find its revenue deficit and state what it implies.
(ii) The imagined government of Revapur has a fiscal deficit of ₹960 crore and a primary deficit of ₹210 crore. Find its interest payments and explain what they show.
questions.solution_md: Two small calculations, each with a meaning.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Revenue deficit = 1,510 − 1,240 = **₹270 crore**. Shailpur's current spending on salaries, pensions and subsidies is larger than its current income, so it must **borrow or sell assets** to meet the gap. Its debt therefore grows **without creating assets** that could earn income, and interest will rise in later years.
(ii) Interest = 960 − 210 = **₹750 crore**. So most of Revapur's borrowing this year goes to **service past debt**: only ₹210 crore of it finances **present programmes**. The large interest bill shows that earlier deficits now weigh heavily on its budget.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain the classification of government receipts and expenditure into revenue and capital, giving the test and two examples for each of the four heads.
(ii) The imagined Republic of Hemavati expects (₹ crore): tax revenue 2,400; non-tax revenue 600; recovery of loans 150; disinvestment 250; revenue expenditure 3,700, including interest 900; capital expenditure 1,100. Calculate its revenue, fiscal and primary deficits, and comment on what they show.
questions.solution_md: Four heads with tests and examples; three deficits with interpretation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Revenue receipts** create no liability and reduce no asset: taxes such as income tax and GST, and non-tax items such as fees and dividends. **Capital receipts** create a liability or reduce an asset: borrowing from the public, and recovery of loans or disinvestment. **Revenue expenditure** creates no asset and reduces no liability: salaries, pensions, interest and subsidies. **Capital expenditure** creates an asset or reduces a liability: building highways and hospitals, giving loans, and repaying debt.
(ii) **Revenue deficit** = 3,700 − 3,000 = **₹700 crore**. **Fiscal deficit** = 4,800 − (3,000 + 400) = **₹1,400 crore**, which is the year's borrowing. **Primary deficit** = 1,400 − 900 = **₹500 crore**. Half of the borrowing (700 of 1,400) covers **current spending**, and ₹900 crore of it pays **interest on past debt**, so only a small part builds assets. Hemavati should **narrow the revenue deficit** so that its borrowing goes into capital projects.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain the meaning of balanced, surplus and deficit budgets, and why a government in a slump might choose a deficit budget.
(ii) The imagined state of Neelachal has a revenue surplus of ₹150 crore and a fiscal deficit of ₹400 crore, while the imagined state of Saraswatipur has a revenue deficit of ₹450 crore and a fiscal deficit of ₹900 crore. Evaluate which state's borrowing is of better quality.
questions.solution_md: Three budget types and the slump case; compare the quality of borrowing.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) In a **balanced** budget, estimated receipts other than borrowing **equal** estimated expenditure; in a **surplus** budget they **exceed** it; in a **deficit** budget expenditure **exceeds** them and the gap is borrowed. In a **slump**, demand, output and jobs are low. A deficit budget lets the government **spend more or tax less**, which adds to aggregate demand and, through the multiplier, raises income and employment; a balanced budget would hold spending down just when the economy needs a push.
(ii) **Neelachal** covers all its current spending from current income and borrows ₹400 crore only to **build assets**, which can raise future income and help repay the loans. **Saraswatipur** uses 50 per cent of its ₹900 crore borrowing to pay for **current spending**, so half its new debt creates **no assets** and only adds to future interest. Neelachal's borrowing is therefore of **better quality**, even though its fiscal deficit is not small; Saraswatipur should first close its revenue gap.
